title: Inside the Earth
subtitle: An introduction to the layers beneath our feet
summary: Earth is made of several layers with different compositions, temperatures, densities, and physical properties
body: Earth is not made of the same material from its surface to its center, Earth is organized into several major layers, these layers formed as the young planet developed, denser materials moved toward the center, less dense materials remained closer to the surface, the main compositional layers are the crust, mantle, and core, the crust is the thin outer layer where we live, beneath the crust is the mantle, the mantle makes up most of the volume of Earth, at the center is the core, the core is composed mainly of iron and nickel, scientists also describe Earth according to how its materials behave physically, the rigid lithosphere lies above the weaker asthenosphere, understanding these layers is important for earthquake science, earthquakes occur mainly within the rigid outer regions of Earth, heat and slow movement inside Earth contribute to the processes that drive plate tectonics
keyFacts: Earth has distinct internal layers, the main compositional layers are the crust mantle and core, Earth layers differ in composition density temperature and physical behavior, Earth can also be divided into mechanical layers, Earth internal structure is important for understanding plate tectonics and earthquakes
terms: Earth structure, crust, mantle, core, lithosphere, asthenosphere

title: Earth Crust
subtitle: The thin rocky shell at the surface of Earth
summary: The crust is the outermost compositional layer of Earth, it consists mainly of continental crust and oceanic crust
body: The crust is the outermost compositional layer of Earth, it is where people live and where landscapes and oceans exist, the crust represents only a small part of the planet, there are two main kinds of crust, continental crust and oceanic crust, continental crust is generally thicker and less dense than oceanic crust, oceanic crust is generally thinner and denser than continental crust, oceanic crust is composed largely of basaltic rocks, the boundary between the crust and mantle is called the Mohorovicic discontinuity, this boundary is commonly called the Moho, the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle together form part of the lithosphere, the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates, many shallow earthquakes occur within the crust when accumulated stress causes rocks to fracture or existing faults to move
keyFacts: The crust is the outermost compositional layer of Earth, continental crust is generally thicker than oceanic crust, continental crust is generally less dense than oceanic crust, oceanic crust is generally thinner and denser, the boundary between the crust and mantle is called the Moho, many shallow earthquakes occur within the crust
terms: crust, continental crust, oceanic crust, Mohorovicic discontinuity, Moho, basalt, lithosphere

title: Earth Mantle
subtitle: The enormous rocky layer beneath the crust
summary: The mantle is the thick layer between the crust and core, it contains most of the volume of Earth
body: The mantle begins beneath the crust and extends to a depth of about 2900 kilometers, the mantle accounts for most of the volume of Earth, mantle material is predominantly solid rock despite the very high temperatures found at depth, over long geological periods parts of the mantle can deform and flow very slowly, heat from the interior of Earth contributes to movement within the mantle, this movement is connected to the larger system of plate tectonics, other forces including slab pull also contribute to plate movement, the uppermost mantle is relatively rigid and forms part of the lithosphere, a weaker region below the lithosphere is called the asthenosphere, deeper mantle regions experience enormous pressure, minerals within the mantle can change structure as pressure and temperature increase, the mantle is not a giant underground ocean of liquid magma, most of the mantle is solid material that can slowly deform over geological time
keyFacts: The mantle lies between the crust and core, the mantle extends to about 2900 kilometers below the surface, most mantle material is solid, mantle rock can slowly deform over geological time, heat moves through the mantle, mantle processes are connected to plate tectonics
terms: mantle, upper mantle, lower mantle, mantle flow, convection, slab pull, solid rock

title: Earth Core
subtitle: The metallic center of Earth
summary: The core is a dense and extremely hot region at the center of Earth, it consists of a liquid outer core and a solid inner core
body: At the center of Earth is the core, the core is a dense region composed mainly of iron with nickel and other elements, the core begins about 2900 kilometers below the surface, the core is divided into the outer core and the inner core, the outer core is liquid, movement of electrically conducting material within the outer core generates most of the magnetic field of Earth, this process is known as the geodynamo, deeper inside Earth the pressure becomes extremely high, this enormous pressure allows the inner core to remain solid despite its very high temperature, seismic waves provide important evidence about the structure of the core, S waves do not travel through the liquid outer core, P waves can travel through the outer core but their speed and direction change, observations of seismic waves helped scientists determine that the core is different from the surrounding mantle
keyFacts: The core is located at the center of Earth, the core is composed mainly of iron, the outer core is liquid, the inner core is solid, movement within the outer core helps generate the magnetic field of Earth, seismic waves provide evidence about the structure of the core
terms: core, outer core, inner core, iron, nickel, geodynamo, magnetic field, P waves, S waves

title: The Lithosphere
subtitle: The rigid outer shell of Earth and the home of tectonic plates
summary: The lithosphere is the strong outer mechanical layer of Earth, it is divided into tectonic plates that move relative to one another
body: The lithosphere is the rigid outer mechanical layer of Earth, it includes the crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle, the term lithosphere describes how this material behaves physically, the lithosphere is strong enough to behave as a collection of relatively rigid plates over geological time, these tectonic plates move slowly relative to one another, where plates move toward each other move apart or slide past each other stress can accumulate, earthquakes are common around many plate boundaries, earthquakes can also occur within tectonic plates particularly around existing faults and zones of weakness, the lithosphere varies in thickness and characteristics between oceanic and continental regions, understanding the lithosphere is important in earthquake science because most earthquakes occur within the lithosphere, earthquakes associated with descending tectonic plates can occur at depths of hundreds of kilometers
keyFacts: The lithosphere includes the crust and rigid uppermost mantle, the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates, tectonic plates move relative to one another, many earthquakes occur near plate boundaries, earthquakes can also occur within tectonic plates
terms: lithosphere, tectonic plate, rigid layer, plate boundary, intraplate earthquake, crust, upper mantle

title: The Asthenosphere
subtitle: The weaker region beneath the rigid lithosphere
summary: The asthenosphere is a mechanically weak region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere, its material can deform slowly over geological time
body: Beneath the lithosphere is a mechanically weaker region of the upper mantle called the asthenosphere, the asthenosphere is not a global ocean of molten rock, most asthenospheric material is solid, high temperature and pressure allow this material to deform more readily than the rigid lithosphere above, over long periods this material can flow slowly, the mechanical difference between the strong lithosphere and weaker asthenosphere is important to plate tectonics, this difference helps allow rigid tectonic plates to move as part of the dynamic outer system of Earth, seismic wave behavior changes within parts of the upper mantle, scientists use these changes to investigate the asthenosphere, the depth and thickness of the asthenosphere vary geographically, the asthenosphere demonstrates that solid rock can slowly flow when movement occurs over millions of years
keyFacts: The asthenosphere lies beneath the lithosphere, the asthenosphere is mechanically weaker than the lithosphere, most asthenospheric material is solid, solid mantle rock can slowly deform, the asthenosphere is important to plate tectonics
terms: asthenosphere, upper mantle, lithosphere, mantle flow, deformation, tectonic plates

title: How We Know What Is Inside Earth
subtitle: Using earthquake waves to investigate the interior of Earth
summary: Scientists use seismic waves and other evidence to investigate the internal structure of Earth without directly reaching the deep interior
body: Humans have never drilled close to the core of Earth, scientists therefore investigate the deep interior using indirect evidence, one of the most important tools is seismology, seismology is the study of earthquakes and seismic waves, earthquakes generate different types of waves that travel through Earth, P waves can travel through solids and liquids, S waves travel through solids but do not travel through liquids, seismic waves change speed and direction when they encounter materials with different physical properties, seismic waves can also be reflected from boundaries inside Earth, networks of seismometers record when seismic waves arrive at different locations around the world, patterns in these recordings reveal boundaries between major internal layers, the absence of direct S waves through the outer core provided important evidence that the outer core is liquid, changes in P wave behavior also provide information about the mantle and core, scientists combine seismic observations with laboratory experiments gravity measurements magnetic observations mineral physics and studies of meteorites to develop models of the interior of Earth
keyFacts: Scientists cannot directly observe most of the deep interior of Earth, seismic waves are important tools for studying Earth structure, P waves travel through solids and liquids, S waves do not travel through liquids, changes in seismic wave behavior reveal boundaries inside Earth, seismic evidence helped demonstrate that the outer core is liquid
terms: seismology, seismic waves, P waves, S waves, seismometer, refraction, reflection, seismic discontinuity, Earth interior

title: What Is Plate Tectonics
subtitle: How large moving plates shape the surface of Earth
summary: Plate tectonics describes the movement of large rigid sections of the lithosphere across the surface of Earth
body: The outer rigid part of Earth is divided into large sections called tectonic plates, these plates form part of the lithosphere, tectonic plates move slowly relative to one another, most plate movement occurs at rates of only a few centimeters each year, even this slow movement can produce enormous geological changes over millions of years, interactions between plates create many earthquakes volcanoes mountain ranges ocean trenches and ocean ridges, plate tectonics provides a framework for understanding much of the geological activity observed at the surface of Earth, the movement of plates is connected to processes within the mantle and forces acting on the plates
keyFacts: The lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates, tectonic plates move relative to one another, plate movement is usually measured in centimeters per year, plate interactions produce many earthquakes and volcanoes, plate tectonics helps explain major geological features
terms: plate tectonics, tectonic plate, lithosphere, plate movement, geological activity, mantle

title: Major Tectonic Plates
subtitle: The large moving sections of the lithosphere
summary: The surface of Earth is divided into several major tectonic plates and many smaller plates
body: Tectonic plates vary greatly in size, some plates extend beneath both continents and oceans, several of the largest plates include the Pacific Plate North American Plate South American Plate African Plate Eurasian Plate Antarctic Plate and Indo Australian region of plates, there are also many smaller plates and microplates, plate boundaries do not simply follow coastlines, a continent can form only part of a much larger tectonic plate, the Pacific Plate for example is primarily oceanic, the boundaries between plates form a global network of tectonically active regions, understanding the locations of these plates helps explain the geographic distribution of many earthquakes volcanoes mountain systems and deep ocean trenches
keyFacts: Earth contains several major tectonic plates, Earth also contains smaller plates and microplates, tectonic plate boundaries do not usually follow coastlines, plates can contain both continental and oceanic lithosphere, many earthquakes occur near the boundaries between plates
terms: major tectonic plates, Pacific Plate, North American Plate, South American Plate, African Plate, Eurasian Plate, Antarctic Plate, microplate

title: How Tectonic Plates Move
subtitle: Understanding the slow movement of the lithosphere
summary: Tectonic plates move slowly across Earth as forces connected with the cooling and internal dynamics of the planet act on the lithosphere
body: Tectonic plates are constantly moving although their movement is extremely slow compared with everyday motion, typical rates are measured in millimeters or centimeters per year, over millions of years these small movements can move continents across large distances and create or destroy ocean basins, plate movement is part of a complex system driven by heat loss and gravity within Earth, important forces include the sinking of dense oceanic lithosphere at subduction zones and gravitational forces associated with elevated ocean ridges, movement within the mantle is also part of the larger tectonic system, different plates move at different speeds and in different directions, modern satellite measurements allow scientists to measure present plate movement with high precision
keyFacts: Tectonic plates are continuously moving, plate movement is usually very slow, different plates move at different speeds, plate movement becomes significant over geological time, gravity and Earth internal dynamics contribute to plate movement, satellites can measure modern plate movement
terms: plate movement, plate velocity, slab pull, ridge forces, mantle dynamics, satellite measurement, geological time

title: Continental Drift
subtitle: The early idea that continents move across Earth
summary: Continental drift was an important early scientific idea proposing that continents move and were once joined together
body: Before modern plate tectonics scientists noticed evidence that continents had changed position over geological time, Alfred Wegener presented the continental drift hypothesis during the early twentieth century, he proposed that continents had once been joined and later moved apart, similarities between fossils rocks mountain belts and ancient climate evidence on continents separated by oceans supported the idea that these landmasses had once been connected, the shapes of continental margins also suggested relationships between some continents, the hypothesis initially lacked a convincing physical mechanism for continental movement, later discoveries involving the ocean floor seafloor spreading global earthquake patterns and magnetic evidence provided the foundation for modern plate tectonics, continental drift is now understood as a consequence of the movement of tectonic plates rather than continents independently moving through oceanic crust
keyFacts: Continents change position over geological time, Alfred Wegener developed the continental drift hypothesis, matching fossils and rocks provided evidence for former continental connections, early continental drift lacked a convincing movement mechanism, modern plate tectonics explains continental movement
terms: continental drift, Alfred Wegener, continents, fossils, geological evidence, plate tectonics, continental movement

title: Seafloor Spreading
subtitle: How new oceanic crust forms at ocean ridges
summary: Seafloor spreading creates new oceanic crust at divergent boundaries where tectonic plates move apart
body: Seafloor spreading occurs mainly along mid ocean ridges where tectonic plates move away from one another, hot mantle material rises beneath these regions and magma can reach the crust, as magma cools it forms new oceanic crust, continued formation of crust causes older oceanic lithosphere to move away from the ridge, evidence for seafloor spreading includes the age pattern of oceanic crust and magnetic patterns recorded in rocks on the ocean floor, younger oceanic crust is generally found near spreading ridges and progressively older crust occurs farther away, seafloor spreading helped provide the mechanism needed to explain how continents and tectonic plates could change position over time, oceanic lithosphere created at spreading centers can eventually be returned to the mantle at subduction zones
keyFacts: New oceanic crust forms at spreading centers, seafloor spreading occurs at divergent boundaries, mid ocean ridges are major spreading centers, oceanic crust becomes older away from many ridges, magnetic patterns provide evidence for seafloor spreading, old oceanic lithosphere can be recycled at subduction zones
terms: seafloor spreading, mid ocean ridge, oceanic crust, divergent boundary, magma, magnetic patterns, spreading center

title: Subduction
subtitle: How one tectonic plate descends beneath another
summary: Subduction occurs where one tectonic plate descends beneath another and moves into the mantle
body: Subduction occurs at some convergent plate boundaries, dense oceanic lithosphere bends and descends beneath another tectonic plate, the descending plate is called a slab, subduction zones are among the most geologically active regions on Earth, they can produce powerful earthquakes deep ocean trenches volcanic arcs and mountain building, earthquakes occur as the descending plate and surrounding rocks deform and move, earthquake activity can extend hundreds of kilometers into Earth along the descending slab, some of the largest earthquakes ever measured occur along the contact between subducting and overriding plates, these large faults are commonly called megathrust faults, sudden vertical movement of the ocean floor during large subduction earthquakes can also generate tsunamis
keyFacts: Subduction occurs at some convergent boundaries, oceanic lithosphere can descend into the mantle, the descending plate is called a slab, subduction zones produce many earthquakes, megathrust earthquakes occur at subduction zones, some subduction earthquakes can generate tsunamis
terms: subduction, subduction zone, slab, convergent boundary, ocean trench, megathrust fault, volcanic arc, tsunami

title: Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes
subtitle: Why many earthquakes occur near plate boundaries
summary: Most earthquakes are associated with tectonic activity and many are concentrated near boundaries between moving plates
body: The global distribution of earthquakes is closely related to plate tectonics, tectonic plates constantly move relative to one another, their boundaries contain many faults where rocks can become locked by friction, plate movement can continue while a fault remains locked, this causes elastic strain and stress to accumulate in surrounding rocks, when the stress becomes greater than the resistance holding the fault in place the fault can suddenly slip, energy is released as seismic waves and an earthquake occurs, different plate boundary environments produce different patterns of earthquakes, divergent boundaries commonly produce shallow earthquakes, transform boundaries also commonly produce shallow earthquakes, subduction zones can produce earthquakes ranging from shallow to very deep, earthquakes can also occur within tectonic plates away from active plate boundaries
keyFacts: Many earthquakes occur near tectonic plate boundaries, faults can remain locked while plates continue moving, stress can accumulate around locked faults, sudden fault movement releases seismic energy, different plate boundaries produce different earthquake patterns, earthquakes can also occur inside tectonic plates
terms: plate tectonics, earthquake, fault, seismic energy, stress, strain, plate boundary, intraplate earthquake

title: Plate Tectonics and Volcanoes
subtitle: Why many volcanoes occur near tectonic boundaries
summary: Many volcanoes are associated with tectonic plate boundaries where geological processes allow magma to rise toward the surface
body: Volcanic activity is strongly connected with plate tectonics, at divergent boundaries plates move apart and hot mantle material rises beneath the opening, reduced pressure can allow melting and magma formation, this process produces extensive volcanic activity along mid ocean ridges and some continental rifts, at subduction zones water and other volatile materials released from the descending plate contribute to melting within the mantle above the slab, magma produced in these environments can rise and create chains of volcanoes called volcanic arcs, not every volcano occurs directly at a plate boundary, some volcanic regions form within plates and are associated with mantle hotspots, the global distribution of volcanoes therefore reflects both plate boundary processes and other geological mechanisms
keyFacts: Many volcanoes occur near plate boundaries, divergent boundaries produce volcanic activity, subduction zones can produce volcanic arcs, magma forms through different geological processes, some volcanoes occur within tectonic plates, hotspots can produce intraplate volcanism
terms: volcano, magma, volcanic arc, divergent boundary, subduction zone, hotspot, mantle, plate tectonics

title: How Plate Motion Is Measured
subtitle: Using modern technology to observe tectonic movement
summary: Scientists use satellite based positioning and geological evidence to measure how tectonic plates move
body: Tectonic plate movement is slow but modern instruments can measure it directly, satellite based positioning systems allow scientists to repeatedly determine the positions of stations installed on the surface of Earth, changes in station positions reveal how different regions are moving over time, measurements can detect movement of only a few millimeters per year, scientists can compare stations located on different tectonic plates to calculate relative plate motion, measurements near active faults can also reveal how strain accumulates between earthquakes, geological evidence provides information about plate movement over much longer periods, magnetic patterns on the ocean floor ages of rocks fault offsets and other geological features help reconstruct ancient plate motion, combining modern measurements with geological evidence allows scientists to study both current and past tectonic movement
keyFacts: Modern instruments can directly measure plate movement, satellite positioning can detect very small movements, plate motion is commonly measured in millimeters or centimeters per year, measurements around faults can reveal strain accumulation, geological evidence records ancient plate movement
terms: plate motion, satellite positioning, GPS, GNSS, geodesy, fault movement, strain accumulation, plate velocity

title: The Changing Surface of Earth
subtitle: How plate tectonics reshapes the planet over geological time
summary: Continuous tectonic plate movement changes the positions of continents and oceans and creates major geological features over millions of years
body: The surface of Earth is constantly changing over geological time, tectonic plates move continents create new oceanic crust recycle old oceanic lithosphere and deform the edges of continents, when continents collide large mountain systems can form, when continents separate new ocean basins can eventually develop, subduction can destroy oceanic lithosphere while spreading centers create new oceanic crust, these processes change the size and shape of oceans over millions of years, continents that are widely separated today were once connected in earlier geological configurations, plate movement can eventually assemble large continental masses and later separate them again, earthquakes and volcanic activity are short term expressions of this much larger geological system, studying plate tectonics allows scientists to reconstruct past geography and understand how the surface of Earth continues to change
keyFacts: The surface of Earth changes over geological time, plate movement changes the positions of continents, new oceanic crust forms at spreading centers, oceanic lithosphere is recycled at subduction zones, continental collisions can build mountains, plate tectonics changes the geography of Earth over millions of years
terms: geological time, continental movement, ocean basin, mountain building, subduction, seafloor spreading, plate reconstruction, plate tectonics

title: What Are Plate Boundaries
subtitle: The regions where tectonic plates meet
summary: Plate boundaries are regions where tectonic plates meet and move relative to one another
body: The lithosphere of Earth is divided into tectonic plates, the regions where these plates meet are called plate boundaries, plate boundaries are important because much of the geological activity on Earth is concentrated around them, tectonic plates can move toward one another move away from one another or slide past one another, these different movements create three major types of plate boundaries, convergent boundaries divergent boundaries and transform boundaries, plate boundaries are often broad zones rather than perfectly narrow lines, earthquakes are common around many plate boundaries because plate movement creates stress within rocks and faults, volcanoes mountain ranges ocean trenches and ocean ridges are also associated with particular types of plate boundaries
keyFacts: Plate boundaries are regions where tectonic plates meet, plates can move together apart or past one another, there are three major types of plate boundaries, many earthquakes occur near plate boundaries, plate boundaries can form broad zones of deformation
terms: plate boundary, convergent boundary, divergent boundary, transform boundary, tectonic plate, lithosphere, deformation

title: Convergent Plate Boundaries
subtitle: Where tectonic plates move toward one another
summary: Convergent boundaries occur where tectonic plates move toward one another and the lithosphere is compressed
body: A convergent plate boundary forms where two tectonic plates move toward one another, what happens at the boundary depends strongly on the type and density of the lithosphere involved, oceanic lithosphere can descend beneath another plate through subduction, two continental regions can collide and produce extensive deformation and mountain building, convergent boundaries are associated with some of the most powerful geological processes on Earth, large earthquakes can occur where plates become locked and stress accumulates, subduction zones can also produce deep ocean trenches volcanic arcs and earthquakes at many different depths, some of the largest earthquakes ever recorded occurred at convergent plate boundaries
keyFacts: Convergent boundaries occur where plates move toward one another, compression is common at convergent boundaries, subduction can occur at convergent boundaries, continental collision can build mountains, very large earthquakes can occur at convergent boundaries
terms: convergent boundary, convergence, compression, subduction, continental collision, megathrust earthquake, mountain building

title: Oceanic And Continental Convergence
subtitle: When oceanic lithosphere meets continental lithosphere
summary: Oceanic and continental convergence commonly causes dense oceanic lithosphere to descend beneath continental lithosphere
body: When oceanic lithosphere converges with continental lithosphere the denser oceanic plate commonly bends and descends beneath the continent, this process is called subduction, a deep ocean trench can develop near the boundary, earthquakes occur along and around the descending slab as rocks deform and faults move, water and other volatile materials released from the descending plate contribute to melting within the mantle above the slab, magma can rise toward the surface and contribute to the formation of volcanic chains on the continent, compression can also deform and uplift the continental margin, this type of boundary can produce powerful earthquakes volcanic eruptions landslides and tsunamis
keyFacts: Oceanic lithosphere can subduct beneath continental lithosphere, ocean trenches can form near subduction zones, earthquakes occur around the descending slab, volcanic chains can form above subduction zones, large subduction earthquakes can generate tsunamis
terms: oceanic continental convergence, subduction, oceanic plate, continental plate, ocean trench, volcanic arc, earthquake, tsunami

title: Oceanic And Oceanic Convergence
subtitle: When one oceanic plate descends beneath another
summary: Oceanic and oceanic convergence can produce subduction zones deep ocean trenches volcanic island arcs and powerful earthquakes
body: When two regions of oceanic lithosphere converge one plate can descend beneath the other, the descending plate enters the mantle at a subduction zone, a deep ocean trench commonly forms near the boundary, earthquakes occur along the contact between the plates and within the descending slab, melting processes above the slab can produce magma, this magma can rise through the overriding plate and create a chain of volcanic islands, this feature is called a volcanic island arc, large earthquakes at these boundaries can suddenly move the ocean floor, this movement can displace large volumes of seawater and generate tsunamis
keyFacts: One oceanic plate can subduct beneath another, deep ocean trenches can form at oceanic subduction zones, volcanic island arcs can develop above subduction zones, earthquakes can occur at many depths, large earthquakes can generate tsunamis
terms: oceanic oceanic convergence, subduction zone, ocean trench, island arc, volcanic island, megathrust earthquake, tsunami

title: Continental Collision
subtitle: What happens when continental regions converge
summary: Continental collision occurs when buoyant continental lithosphere converges and produces intense deformation and mountain building
body: Continental collision can occur after an ocean between two continental regions has been reduced or closed by plate movement, continental lithosphere is relatively buoyant and does not easily descend deeply into the mantle, when continental regions collide the crust can shorten thicken fold and fracture, large mountain systems can develop as rocks are uplifted and deformed, major faults form throughout the collision zone and can generate damaging earthquakes, deformation can extend across a very broad region rather than remaining at one narrow boundary, volcanic activity associated directly with subduction can decrease after major continental collision develops, continental collision demonstrates that plate boundaries can be wide and structurally complex regions
keyFacts: Continental collision occurs where continental regions converge, continental crust can shorten and thicken, collision can produce major mountain systems, large faults develop within collision zones, damaging earthquakes can occur across broad regions of deformation
terms: continental collision, continental crust, convergence, mountain building, crustal shortening, deformation, faulting

title: Divergent Plate Boundaries
subtitle: Where tectonic plates move away from one another
summary: Divergent boundaries occur where tectonic plates move apart and new crust can form
body: A divergent plate boundary occurs where two tectonic plates move away from one another, these boundaries are especially common beneath the oceans along mid ocean ridges, as plates separate hot mantle material rises beneath the spreading region, reduced pressure can contribute to melting and the formation of magma, magma can cool and form new oceanic crust, this process is called seafloor spreading, divergent boundaries also occur within continents where stretching can create rift zones, earthquakes at divergent boundaries are usually shallow because deformation occurs close to the surface, volcanic activity is also common in many divergent environments
keyFacts: Divergent boundaries occur where plates move apart, new oceanic crust forms at many divergent boundaries, seafloor spreading occurs along mid ocean ridges, continental rifts can form where continents are stretched, earthquakes at divergent boundaries are usually shallow
terms: divergent boundary, divergence, seafloor spreading, mid ocean ridge, continental rift, magma, oceanic crust

title: Transform Plate Boundaries
subtitle: Where tectonic plates slide past one another
summary: Transform boundaries occur where tectonic plates move horizontally past one another and commonly produce shallow earthquakes
body: A transform plate boundary occurs where tectonic plates slide horizontally past one another, crust is generally neither created nor destroyed by the main transform movement, transform boundaries contain major faults that accommodate horizontal plate motion, sections of these faults can become locked because of friction, plate movement can continue while a locked fault remains stationary, this causes stress and elastic strain to accumulate, when the fault suddenly slips stored energy is released and an earthquake occurs, earthquakes at transform boundaries are generally shallow but they can be highly damaging when faults pass near populated regions, transform faults also occur beneath oceans where they connect sections of spreading ridges
keyFacts: Transform boundaries occur where plates slide past one another, transform motion is mainly horizontal, crust is generally neither created nor destroyed by transform motion, transform faults can become locked, transform boundaries commonly produce shallow earthquakes
terms: transform boundary, transform fault, strike slip motion, horizontal movement, fault locking, shallow earthquake, friction

title: Plate Boundaries And Earthquake Depth
subtitle: Why earthquake depths differ between tectonic environments
summary: The depth of earthquakes varies between plate boundary environments and provides information about tectonic processes beneath the surface
body: Earthquake depth is strongly related to tectonic setting, divergent boundaries mainly produce shallow earthquakes because faulting and deformation occur within the relatively shallow lithosphere near spreading centers, transform boundaries also mainly produce shallow earthquakes, subduction zones are different because one plate descends deep into the mantle, earthquakes can occur within and around the descending slab at progressively greater depths, these earthquakes can define an inclined zone of seismic activity beneath the overriding plate, some earthquakes within subduction zones occur hundreds of kilometers below the surface, very deep earthquakes are therefore strongly associated with descending slabs, scientists use earthquake locations and depths to investigate the geometry of tectonic plates beneath the surface
keyFacts: Divergent boundaries mainly produce shallow earthquakes, transform boundaries mainly produce shallow earthquakes, subduction zones produce earthquakes across a large range of depths, deep earthquakes are associated with descending slabs, earthquake depth helps scientists investigate plate geometry
terms: earthquake depth, shallow earthquake, deep earthquake, subduction zone, descending slab, seismic zone, plate geometry

title: What Is a Fault
subtitle: A fracture where rocks move relative to one another
summary: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures in rock where movement has occurred
body: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures within rock where blocks of rock have moved relative to one another, faults can range from small features to enormous systems extending for hundreds of kilometers, tectonic forces create stress within the crust and upper lithosphere, when stress causes rocks to break or existing fractures to move displacement can occur along a fault, some faults move gradually while others remain locked for long periods, a locked fault can accumulate stress until sudden movement occurs, sudden fault movement releases energy as seismic waves and produces an earthquake, faults are therefore fundamental to understanding where and how many earthquakes occur
keyFacts: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures, movement occurs across a fault, faults can vary greatly in size, faults can remain locked for long periods, sudden fault movement can produce earthquakes
terms: fault, fracture, fault zone, displacement, rock movement, earthquake, tectonic stress

title: Normal Faults
subtitle: Faults created where the crust is being extended
summary: Normal faults commonly form where tectonic forces stretch and extend the crust
body: A normal fault is a type of dip slip fault commonly associated with extension of the crust, the fault surface is inclined rather than vertical, the block above the fault surface is called the hanging wall, the block below the fault surface is called the footwall, during normal fault movement the hanging wall moves downward relative to the footwall, normal faults are common in regions where the lithosphere is being stretched, they occur in continental rifts and other extensional environments, repeated movement on normal faults can create mountain blocks valleys basins and steep fault scarps, earthquakes occur when accumulated stress causes sudden movement along these faults
keyFacts: Normal faults are associated with extension, the hanging wall moves downward relative to the footwall, normal faults are a type of dip slip fault, normal faults are common in continental rifts, sudden normal fault movement can produce earthquakes
terms: normal fault, dip slip fault, extension, hanging wall, footwall, continental rift, fault scarp

title: Reverse Faults
subtitle: Faults created where the crust is being compressed
summary: Reverse faults commonly form where tectonic forces compress and shorten the crust
body: A reverse fault is a type of dip slip fault associated with compression, the fault surface is inclined and separates a hanging wall from a footwall, during reverse fault movement the hanging wall moves upward relative to the footwall, this movement shortens and thickens the crust, reverse faults occur in many convergent tectonic environments and mountain building regions, movement can deform large areas and contribute to uplift, reverse faults can produce strong earthquakes when accumulated stress is released suddenly, faults with reverse movement and a relatively low angle are commonly described as thrust faults
keyFacts: Reverse faults are associated with compression, the hanging wall moves upward relative to the footwall, reverse movement can shorten the crust, reverse faults occur in many convergent regions, reverse faults can produce strong earthquakes
terms: reverse fault, dip slip fault, compression, hanging wall, footwall, crustal shortening, convergent region

title: Thrust Faults
subtitle: Low angle reverse faults associated with compression
summary: Thrust faults are low angle reverse faults that allow large sections of rock to move over other rocks
body: A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a relatively low angle fault surface, thrust faults develop in regions experiencing strong compression, during movement the hanging wall is pushed upward and over the footwall, this process can shorten and thicken the crust across large regions, thrust faults are common in mountain belts and convergent tectonic environments, some thrust fault systems extend for very large distances and accommodate substantial tectonic movement, megathrust faults at subduction zones are enormous thrust fault systems located along the contact between converging tectonic plates, sudden movement on large thrust and megathrust faults can produce extremely powerful earthquakes
keyFacts: Thrust faults are low angle reverse faults, thrust faults form in compressional environments, the hanging wall moves over the footwall, thrust faulting can shorten and thicken the crust, megathrust faults can produce very large earthquakes
terms: thrust fault, reverse fault, compression, hanging wall, footwall, megathrust fault, subduction zone

title: Strike Slip Faults
subtitle: Faults where blocks move mainly sideways
summary: Strike slip faults involve mainly horizontal movement of rock blocks past one another
body: A strike slip fault is a fault where movement is mainly horizontal and approximately parallel to the fault, blocks of crust on opposite sides of the fault move sideways relative to one another, strike slip faults are common in regions where tectonic plates or crustal blocks move laterally, many transform plate boundaries contain major strike slip faults, strike slip faults can be classified according to the direction of relative movement, right lateral movement means the opposite side appears to move toward the right, left lateral movement means the opposite side appears to move toward the left, large strike slip faults can extend for hundreds of kilometers and produce damaging shallow earthquakes
keyFacts: Strike slip movement is mainly horizontal, blocks move sideways relative to one another, strike slip faults are common at transform boundaries, strike slip faults can be right lateral or left lateral, large strike slip faults can produce damaging earthquakes
terms: strike slip fault, horizontal movement, right lateral fault, left lateral fault, transform boundary, lateral movement, shallow earthquake

title: Oblique Slip Faults

title: Surface Rupture and Ground Deformation
subtitle: How fault movement can permanently change the ground surface
summary: Earthquake fault movement can rupture or deform the ground surface and damage structures that cross the affected area
body: When an earthquake rupture reaches the surface movement along the fault can break and permanently displace the ground, this process is called surface rupture, displacement can occur horizontally vertically or in a combination of directions depending on the fault, roads pipelines fences buildings and other structures that cross the rupture can be offset or damaged, earthquakes can also produce broader ground deformation including uplift subsidence cracking and changes in elevation, surface rupture is usually concentrated near the fault while other deformation can extend across a wider region
keyFacts: Fault rupture can reach the ground surface, surface rupture can permanently displace the ground, displacement can be horizontal or vertical, structures crossing a rupture can be damaged, earthquakes can cause uplift and subsidence, ground deformation can extend beyond the fault trace

title: Tsunamis as an Earthquake Hazard
subtitle: How undersea earthquakes can produce dangerous ocean waves
summary: Some undersea earthquakes can displace large volumes of water and generate tsunamis that threaten coastal areas
body: Large earthquakes beneath or near the ocean can sometimes generate tsunamis, this usually occurs when fault movement causes significant vertical displacement of the seafloor and the water above it, tsunami waves can travel across large ocean basins and become dangerous when they approach shallow coastal water, coastal flooding powerful currents and debris movement can damage communities and infrastructure, not every undersea earthquake generates a tsunami, earthquake magnitude depth fault type rupture geometry and seafloor displacement all influence tsunami potential

title: Cascading Earthquake Hazards
subtitle: How one earthquake hazard can trigger additional problems
summary: Earthquake impacts can develop as chains of connected hazards where one failure creates or increases another
body: Major earthquakes can create several hazards at the same time and these hazards can interact, shaking can damage a pipeline which can contribute to a fire, a landslide can block a river and create a temporary lake that later produces flooding, liquefaction can damage roads bridges and utility systems making emergency response more difficult, a tsunami can carry debris and damage coastal infrastructure after the earthquake shaking has stopped, these connected processes are sometimes described as cascading hazards, understanding the connections between hazards helps communities plan for consequences that extend beyond direct ground shaking
keyFacts: Earthquake hazards can interact, one failure can trigger another hazard, landslides can create flooding hazards, liquefaction can damage transportation and utilities, tsunamis can create additional coastal hazards, cascading effects can complicate emergency response

title: Where Earthquakes Occur
subtitle: Why earthquakes are more common in some parts of the world
summary: Earthquakes occur around the world but most are concentrated in regions where tectonic plates interact and faults are active
body: Earthquakes do not occur evenly across the surface of Earth, most earthquakes are concentrated along tectonic plate boundaries where plates move toward away from or past each other, these movements create stress within the crust and upper mantle, when accumulated stress causes sudden movement along a fault an earthquake occurs, earthquakes can also happen within tectonic plates where ancient or active faults respond to regional stress, maps of global earthquake locations reveal long narrow zones that often follow major plate boundaries
keyFacts: Earthquakes occur around the world, most earthquakes occur near plate boundaries, active faults produce earthquakes, earthquake locations often form narrow geographic zones, earthquakes can also occur within tectonic plates

title: The Pacific Ring of Fire
subtitle: A major zone of earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean
summary: The Pacific Ring of Fire is a broad region around the Pacific Ocean where plate boundaries produce frequent earthquakes and volcanic activity
body: The region surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean contains some of the most active earthquake and volcanic zones on Earth, this broad region is commonly called the Pacific Ring of Fire, several major tectonic plates and many smaller plates interact around the Pacific basin, large sections contain subduction zones where one plate moves beneath another, other sections include transform faults and different types of plate boundaries, these tectonic environments produce frequent earthquakes including many of the largest earthquakes recorded, the Ring of Fire includes active regions near the western coasts of the Americas and around parts of eastern Asia and the western Pacific
keyFacts: The Ring of Fire surrounds much of the Pacific Ocean, the region contains many active plate boundaries, subduction zones are common around the Pacific, many large earthquakes occur in this region, volcanic activity is also widespread, several major and smaller tectonic plates interact around the Pacific

title: Earthquakes at Plate Boundaries
subtitle: How different plate boundaries create different earthquake patterns
summary: Convergent divergent and transform plate boundaries produce different patterns of earthquake location depth and fault movement
body: Plate boundaries are major geographic zones of earthquake activity, convergent boundaries can produce powerful earthquakes where plates collide or one plate moves beneath another, subduction zones can generate earthquakes from shallow depths near the plate boundary to much greater depths within the descending plate, divergent boundaries commonly produce shallow earthquakes where tectonic plates move apart, transform boundaries also produce mainly shallow earthquakes as plates move horizontally past each other, the geographic distribution and depth of earthquakes therefore provide important evidence about the location and structure of plate boundaries
keyFacts: Plate boundaries are major earthquake zones, convergent boundaries can produce very large earthquakes, subduction zones can contain shallow and deep earthquakes, divergent boundaries mainly produce shallow earthquakes, transform boundaries mainly produce shallow earthquakes, earthquake patterns help identify plate boundaries

title: Earthquakes Within Tectonic Plates
subtitle: Why earthquakes can occur far from plate boundaries
summary: Earthquakes can occur within tectonic plates when regional stress causes movement along faults or zones of weakness
body: Although most earthquakes occur near plate boundaries some earthquakes happen far inside tectonic plates, these events are called intraplate earthquakes, tectonic plates contain faults fractures and ancient zones of weakness that can respond to stresses transmitted through the plate, some of these structures formed during much older periods of tectonic activity and can become active again under present stress conditions, intraplate earthquakes are less common than earthquakes along many active plate boundaries but they can still be damaging, regions with relatively infrequent earthquakes can remain exposed to seismic hazard
keyFacts: Some earthquakes occur far from plate boundaries, these events are called intraplate earthquakes, old faults can become active again, stress can travel through tectonic plates, intraplate earthquakes are less common in many regions, areas with infrequent earthquakes can still have seismic hazard

title: Reading Global Earthquake Patterns
subtitle: What earthquake maps reveal about the active Earth
summary: Maps of earthquake locations depths and magnitudes reveal patterns related to tectonic plates faults and active geological regions
body: Plotting earthquakes on a world map reveals patterns that are difficult to see from individual events, clusters and long bands of earthquakes commonly trace tectonic plate boundaries, earthquake depth provides additional information about tectonic processes, shallow earthquakes occur in many environments while deep earthquakes are strongly associated with descending plates at subduction zones, magnitude patterns show where earthquakes of different sizes have occurred but past earthquake locations do not determine exactly where the next earthquake will happen, scientists combine earthquake maps with fault maps plate boundaries geological observations and geodetic measurements to understand active tectonic regions
keyFacts: Earthquake maps reveal geographic patterns, earthquake clusters often follow plate boundaries, depth provides information about tectonic processes, deep earthquakes are associated with subduction zones, past earthquake locations do not exactly predict future events, scientists combine multiple types of geographic and geological data

title: How Earthquakes Affect Buildings
subtitle: Why ground shaking creates forces inside structures
summary: Earthquake ground motion causes buildings to move and creates forces that structural systems must resist
body: During an earthquake the ground beneath a building moves while the mass of the building resists sudden changes in motion, this creates forces within the structure, horizontal shaking is especially important because buildings must resist movement from side to side, vertical motion can also affect structural components, the response of a building depends on its height shape mass materials structural system foundation and the characteristics of the ground motion, buildings that are poorly designed constructed or maintained can experience greater damage, earthquake engineering aims to reduce the likelihood of collapse and protect people during strong shaking
keyFacts: Ground motion creates forces inside buildings, horizontal shaking is important for structural design, vertical motion can also affect structures, building characteristics influence earthquake response, poor construction can increase damage, earthquake engineering aims to reduce collapse risk

title: Earthquake Resistant Design
subtitle: How engineers design structures to perform during strong shaking
summary: Earthquake resistant design uses structural systems materials and connections that help buildings withstand earthquake forces
body: Buildings cannot usually be designed to remain completely unaffected by every possible earthquake, instead engineers design structures to achieve defined levels of performance during shaking, an important goal is preventing catastrophic collapse and protecting occupants, structural systems can include frames walls braces and other components that transfer earthquake forces through the building and into the foundation, strong connections help components work together while ductile materials and details allow controlled deformation without sudden failure, engineers also consider expected ground motion soil conditions building use height shape and local construction requirements
keyFacts: Earthquake resistant design aims to protect occupants, preventing collapse is a major design goal, structural systems transfer earthquake forces, strong connections are important, ductility allows controlled deformation, soil and ground motion influence design

title: Base Isolation and Energy Dissipation
subtitle: Engineering systems that reduce earthquake forces in structures
summary: Base isolation and energy dissipation systems can reduce the amount of earthquake motion and energy transferred into a structure
body: Some structures use specialized systems to reduce their response to earthquake shaking, base isolation places flexible or sliding elements between a structure and its foundation so some ground movement is not transferred directly into the building, this can reduce forces and acceleration within the structure, energy dissipation devices can absorb part of the energy associated with structural movement, these devices are often called dampers, different systems are suitable for different structures and seismic conditions, their design requires careful engineering because the building foundation utilities and structural components must work together during earthquake movement
keyFacts: Base isolation reduces direct transfer of some ground motion, isolation systems allow controlled movement, dampers dissipate energy, reduced acceleration can protect structures and contents, specialized systems require careful engineering, not every structure uses base isolation

title: Building Codes and Seismic Safety
subtitle: How construction requirements reduce earthquake risk
summary: Modern building codes include seismic requirements intended to reduce collapse and improve structural performance during earthquakes
body: Building codes establish minimum requirements for the design and construction of structures, in earthquake prone regions these requirements include provisions for seismic forces materials structural systems foundations and connections, seismic design requirements vary according to expected ground motion soil conditions building type and importance, newer buildings designed under modern codes can have important safety advantages compared with vulnerable older construction, however code requirements do not mean that a building will experience no damage, buildings may be designed to protect life while still requiring significant repair after strong shaking, codes also change as engineering knowledge and earthquake observations improve
keyFacts: Building codes establish minimum construction requirements, seismic codes address earthquake forces, requirements depend on local seismic conditions, modern codes aim to reduce collapse risk, code compliant buildings can still be damaged, building codes evolve with engineering knowledge

title: Retrofitting Existing Buildings
subtitle: Strengthening older structures against earthquake hazards
summary: Seismic retrofitting modifies existing structures to reduce known weaknesses and improve their performance during earthquakes
body: Many buildings were constructed before modern seismic design requirements were introduced, some contain structural weaknesses that can increase the risk of severe earthquake damage, seismic retrofitting involves modifying an existing building to improve its ability to resist earthquake forces, possible improvements include strengthening walls adding braces improving connections reinforcing foundations and securing structural components, the appropriate retrofit depends on the building materials structural system age condition and local earthquake hazard, engineers evaluate the structure before selecting suitable measures, retrofitting cannot eliminate all earthquake risk but it can reduce important vulnerabilities and improve safety
keyFacts: Older buildings can contain seismic weaknesses, retrofitting improves existing structures, walls and braces can be strengthened or added, connections and foundations can be improved, engineers evaluate buildings before retrofitting, retrofitting can reduce earthquake vulnerability

title: Preparing Before an Earthquake
subtitle: Steps that can reduce risk before strong shaking begins
summary: Earthquake preparedness includes identifying hazards securing dangerous items planning for emergencies and knowing how to respond during shaking
body: Preparing before an earthquake can reduce injuries and make recovery easier, identify objects that could fall move or break during strong shaking, secure heavy furniture appliances and other dangerous items when appropriate, learn safe locations in the places where you spend time, prepare essential supplies for possible interruptions to electricity water transportation and communication, create a household communication plan so people know how to contact each other after an emergency, learn local emergency information and practice what to do during earthquake shaking, preparedness should reflect local hazards building conditions and the needs of each household
keyFacts: Preparation can reduce earthquake injuries, secure items that could fall or move, identify safe locations before an earthquake, prepare essential emergency supplies, create a household communication plan, practice earthquake safety actions

title: Drop Cover and Hold On
subtitle: How to protect yourself during earthquake shaking
summary: During earthquake shaking the recommended protective action in many situations is to drop cover and hold on
body: When strong earthquake shaking begins protect yourself immediately, drop to your hands and knees so the shaking is less likely to knock you down, cover your head and neck and if a sturdy table or desk is nearby move beneath it, hold on to your shelter and be prepared to move with it while the shaking continues, if suitable shelter is not available protect your head and neck while staying away from windows and objects that could fall, avoid running outside during strong shaking because falling glass masonry and other debris can create hazards near buildings, protective actions can vary in unusual environments so follow appropriate local safety guidance
keyFacts: Drop before shaking knocks you down, cover your head and neck, shelter under sturdy furniture when available, hold on while shaking continues, stay away from windows and falling objects, avoid running outside during strong shaking

title: What to Do After an Earthquake
subtitle: Staying safe after the strongest shaking has stopped
summary: After an earthquake remain alert for injuries damaged structures utility hazards aftershocks and other dangers
body: When strong shaking stops check yourself and nearby people for injuries when it is safe to do so, remain prepared for aftershocks that can produce additional shaking and damage weakened structures, avoid visibly damaged buildings and areas with falling debris broken glass or unstable materials, damaged electrical systems gas systems and water lines can create additional hazards, follow instructions from local emergency authorities and use reliable information sources, near coastal areas strong or long earthquake shaking can indicate tsunami danger so move away from hazardous coastal areas according to local guidance, communication and transportation systems may be disrupted so use available resources carefully
keyFacts: Check for injuries after shaking stops, expect possible aftershocks, avoid damaged structures, damaged utilities can create hazards, follow local emergency instructions, coastal earthquakes can create tsunami danger

title: Earthquake Emergency Planning
subtitle: Planning for communication supplies evacuation and recovery
summary: An earthquake emergency plan helps households prepare for communication disruptions damaged infrastructure evacuation and other consequences
body: A useful earthquake plan considers what household members may need before during and after an emergency, decide how family members will communicate if normal phone service is disrupted, identify meeting locations and important contacts, understand local evacuation routes and hazards including tsunami zones landslide areas and damaged infrastructure, maintain appropriate emergency supplies such as water food lighting communication equipment medications and basic first aid materials, consider the needs of children older adults people with disabilities and animals, review the plan periodically because household needs contact information and local conditions can change

body: Every major earthquake provides information about how faults rupture how the ground shakes and how communities respond, scientists study earthquake locations depths magnitudes seismic waves surface rupture and aftershock sequences, engineers examine how buildings bridges roads and utility systems performed during shaking, observations of landslides liquefaction fires tsunamis and other hazards reveal how earthquake effects can spread beyond the original fault, emergency organizations study communication evacuation and response challenges, lessons from past earthquakes contribute to improved hazard maps building practices monitoring systems emergency planning and public education

title: How Earthquakes Changed Building Safety

summary: Damage observed during historical earthquakes has helped engineers identify structural weaknesses and improve seismic design practices
body: Historical earthquakes have repeatedly shown that building design materials connections foundations and construction quality strongly influence earthquake performance, damaged structures provide engineers with evidence about how different systems respond to strong ground motion, failures can reveal weaknesses that were not fully understood before an earthquake, engineering research and observations from later events can lead to improved design methods construction requirements and retrofit strategies, older vulnerable structures can remain an important source of risk even where modern construction standards are stronger, studying both damaged and successfully performing buildings helps engineers understand which design features improve safety

title: Learning From Earthquake Disasters
subtitle: Why earthquake consequences depend on more than magnitude
summary: Historical disasters show that earthquake consequences depend on hazard exposure vulnerability preparedness and secondary hazards as well as earthquake size
body: Earthquakes with similar magnitudes can produce very different consequences, historical events show that distance from populated areas earthquake depth local geology building vulnerability population exposure and emergency preparedness all influence impacts, secondary hazards including tsunamis landslides liquefaction and fires can greatly increase losses, damage to roads communication systems hospitals water networks and other infrastructure can make emergency response more difficult, these lessons show why magnitude alone cannot describe earthquake risk, reducing future losses requires scientific monitoring resilient construction preparedness education and planning that considers the different hazards present in each region
